title: What are you doing right now?
goal: Say what's happening right now with ari izan, make phone calls, and talk about how you feel with egon.
bekal: build "-ing" sentences with *-t(z)en ari naiz* and make them negative
tell a habit (*ikasten dut*) from something in progress (*ikasten ari naiz*)
handle a phone call: answer, ask how someone is, and hang up

dialogs.title: Elkarrizketa — Telefonoz
dialogs.intro: Saturday, midday. Budi calls Maite from the euskaltegi library.

lines.text: Kaixo Maite, Budi naiz. Zer ari zara egiten?

notes: **Ari naiz always takes izan, even when the verb has an object.** Here's a pleasant surprise: *euskara ikasten **dut*** (a habit, with *ukan*) but *euskara ikasten ari **naiz*** (in progress, with *izan*). As soon as *ari* comes in, the whole sentence switches to *izan*, and the doer's hat *-k* disappears too: just *ni*, not *nik*.

**Banoa and noa — verbs that stand without an auxiliary.** A handful of Basque verbs have short forms that need no auxiliary at all: *noa* (I'm going), *zoaz* (you're going), *doa* (he/she's going). The prefix *ba-* adds emphasis: *banoa* = "I'm on my way". These are called synthetic verbs; there are only a few, and all of them are very common.

**Futbolean ari dira — ari works with activities too.** Besides the *-t(z)en* form, *ari izan* can attach directly to the name of an activity with the ending *-an*: *futbolean ari dira* (they're playing soccer), *lanean ari naiz* (I'm working), *jolasean ari dira* (they're playing).

**Zain gaude — waiting is a state.** Literally "we are in a state of waiting". Basque uses *egon* + a state word a lot: *zain egon* (to be waiting), *lanpetuta egon* (to be busy), *pozik egon* (to be happy). The third section of this unit collects the most common ones.

blocks.text: The formula fits on one line: **verb in the -t(z)en form + ari + izan**. No doer's hat, no *ukan* auxiliary, whether or not the verb has an object.
*The weather row is a famous exception: rain and snow take *du*, not *da* — *euria ari du*, *elurra ari du*. Basque treats the sky as an unnamed doer. Weather is covered fully in Unit 19.

blocks.title: Typical mistakes of English speakers
items: Using *ari* for habits or longer periods. English says "I'm studying Basque this year"; Basque doesn't use *ari* that way. *Egunero ikasten **ari naiz*** sounds odd — use *egunero ikasten dut*.
Keeping the doer's hat: ***Nik ikasten ari naiz*** is wrong. The right form is *Ni ikasten ari naiz*, or just *Ikasten ari naiz*.
Forgetting that the verb stays in the *-t(z)en* form: *jan ari naiz* is wrong; the right form is *ja**ten** ari naiz*.

head: Euskara
Say it
English
rows: I'd like to speak to Maite.

blocks.text: Notice that Basques answer the phone with *bai?* ("yes?") or *esan!* ("go ahead!", literally "say!"), not with "hello". It may sound very short to an English ear, but that's simply the custom — and it isn't rude at all.

blocks.title: Words you'll see on your phone screen
items: Common texting abbreviations: *eskerrik asko* → *eskrk*, *gero arte* → *g.a.*, *musu bat* ("a kiss", the usual sign-off between friends).

blocks.text: *Egon* means "to be (somewhere or in some state)" — both in a place and in a condition. Its forms need memorizing, and it stands on its own with no auxiliary.

blocks.title: Gose naiz or gose nago?
items: You'll hear both in the street, and both are understood. *Gose naiz* is more standard and more common in books; *gose nago* is also widely used in conversation.
With states ending in *-ta* and *-rik* (*nekatuta*, *gaixorik*, *galduta*), **always** use *egon*: *nekatuta **nago***, not *naiz*.
For permanent traits, **always** use *izan*: *Alaia **naiz*** (I'm a cheerful person) is different from *Pozik **nago*** (I'm happy right now).

exercises.prompt: Change to the "in progress" form with *ari*.
Fill in the blanks with the right form of *egon* (nago, zaude, dago, gaude, zaudete, daude).
Put the words in the right order.
